meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There are two kinds of people in the end: those who say to God, "Thy will be done," and those to whom God says, "Thy will be done."'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely C.S. Lewis, from The Great Divorce (1945). The popular version drops the italics on the second "Thy" — and with them the sentence’s whole meaning.

answer.label: Written by C.S. Lewis
answer.authorDates: 1898–1963 · Oxford and Cambridge literary scholar, novelist and Christian apologist
answer.sourceLine: It is Lewis, from chapter 9 of The Great Divorce, serialised in the Anglican newspaper The Guardian across 1944 and 1945 and published as a book in 1945. Wikiquote’s sourced section transcribes it inside its dialogue: asked “But what of the poor Ghosts who never get into the omnibus at all?”, the reply is “Everyone who wishes it does. Never fear. There are only two kinds of people in the end: those who say to God, ‘Thy will be done,’ and those to whom God says, in the end, ‘Thy will be done.’ All that are in Hell, choose it.” The popular version drops the word “only”, drops the second “in the end”, and — most damagingly — drops the italics on the second “Thy”. Without that emphasis the sentence reads as though God says the same thing back; with it, God is conceding, and the second group get exactly what they insisted on.
answer.confidenceText: Verified in chapter 9 — but the popular version drops “only” and the italics that carry the point

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Serialised in The Guardian, an Anglican newspaper, across 1944–1945; in book form in 1945 by Geoffrey Bles
Ch. 9 — spoken in dialogue, answering the narrator’s question about the Ghosts who never board the bus

source.excerpt: ‘But what of the poor Ghosts who never get into the omnibus at all?’ — ‘Everyone who wishes it does. Never fear. There are only two kinds of people in the end: those who say to God, “Thy will be done,” and those to whom God says, in the end, “Thy will be done.” All that are in Hell, choose it. Without that self-choice there could be no Hell. No soul that seriously and constantly desires joy will ever miss it. Those who seek find. To those who knock it is opened.’
trail: The sentence in full, as Wikiquote’s sourced section prints it: “There are only two kinds of people in the end: those who say to God, ‘Thy will be done,’ and those to whom God says, in the end, ‘Thy will be done.’” Three elements — “only”, the repeated “in the end”, and the italicised “Thy” — are missing from the version that circulates — compare the transcription ↗.

It is dialogue. Wikiquote prints it as an answer to the narrator’s question about the Ghosts who never get on the bus, which is why it begins “Everyone who wishes it does. Never fear.” It is a character speaking inside a novel, not Lewis pronouncing in a work of apologetics — which does not make it less his view, but is worth knowing before quoting it as doctrine. Through this stretch of the book the narrator’s guide is a character Lewis builds out of the Victorian writer George MacDonald, set up as his Virgil — Wikipedia on the book’s structure ↗.

The book. The Great Divorce ran as a serial in the Anglican paper The Guardian in 1944 and 1945 and appeared as a book in 1945. Its title answers Blake’s The Marriage of Heaven and Hell ↗: Lewis’s argument is that heaven and hell do not marry, and that the divorce is chosen from the hell side — Wikipedia’s article ↗.

What could not be checked. The book is in copyright. The Internet Archive holds the 1946 Macmillan American edition, but the item is access-restricted and its text cannot be downloaded, so this page rests on Wikiquote’s sourced transcription rather than a page image read here — the catalogue record ↗.
source.excerptNote: As transcribed in Wikiquote’s sourced section for The Great Divorce ↗, attributed there to chapter 9. Two things the excerpt restores: the sentence is a reply in a conversation, not Lewis pronouncing in his own voice; and the italics fall on the second “Thy”. The closing lines are Lewis quoting Matthew 7:7–8.

author.name: C.S. Lewis
author.heading: About C.S. Lewis
author.metaLine: 1898–1963 · Irish-born British literary scholar, novelist and Christian apologist
author.bio: Clive Staples Lewis was born in Belfast in 1898 and taught English literature for nearly forty years — as a fellow and tutor at Magdalen College, Oxford from 1925, then in the Cambridge chair of Medieval and Renaissance Literature from 1954 until his death in 1963. The Great Divorce belongs to his wartime run of imaginative theology, alongside The Screwtape Letters and the broadcast talks that became Mere Christianity: arguments about heaven, hell and choice, made in stories rather than syllogisms because he thought the stories were harder to argue with.

misattribution.heading: Right author, three missing words
misattribution.intro: Nobody is falsely credited here. The damage is done by what the popular version leaves out — and one of the omissions turns the sentence into a tautology.

items.why: This is the whole sentence. Lewis italicises the second “Thy” so that the two halves are opposites, not an echo: the first group surrender their will, the second have theirs granted. Strip the emphasis and God appears to say the same words back, which is not a judgement but a repetition — the italics are in Wikiquote’s transcription ↗.
Lewis wrote “There are only two kinds of people in the end”. The word is doing work: he is closing off third options, which is the point of a book arguing that nobody ends up in hell by accident.
Lewis repeats it — “those to whom God says, in the end” — to mark that the concession comes last, after every refusal. The shortened version loses the sense of a long argument finally conceded.

items.who: Lewis speaking in his own voice
items.why: It is a line of dialogue in a novel, answering a question about the Ghosts who never board the bus, not a proposition from one of Lewis’s works of apologetics. That does not make it less his view — he clearly means it — but it is spoken by a character, in an argument — Wikipedia on the book’s premise ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest summary: this is C.S. Lewis, chapter 9 of The Great Divorce (1945), quoted a little short. If you print it, print the italics — the full sentence is here ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The Great Divorce is Lewis’s answer to a specific objection: that a good God would not permit hell. His reply is that hell is not a sentence handed down but a preference honoured. The book stages it as a bus trip — ghosts ride out from a grey, drizzling city to the foothills of heaven, are invited to stay, and almost all of them find a reason to go back.

The sentence people quote is the thesis of that argument in one line, which is why it has outlived the novel around it. It is also why the italics matter so much: Lewis is not saying God condemns the second group. He is saying God finally stops arguing with them.
detailsBody: The title responds to William Blake’s The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, which had proposed that the two are complementary. Lewis thought this was the comfortable modern error — that everything can be reconciled if you are generous enough about it — and wrote a book in which the reconciliation is offered on every page and declined every time.

The narrator’s guide through this stretch of the book is a character Lewis builds out of George MacDonald, the Victorian Scottish writer, cast in the role Virgil plays for Dante. The passage quoted here sits in chapter 9, where the guide does most of the explaining.
context.pull: Lewis italicised the second "Thy". Without it the sentence says nothing at all.

There are only two kinds of people in the end: those who say to God, ‘Thy will be done,’ and those to whom God says, in the end, ‘Thy will be done.’ All that are in Hell, choose it.", with the second "Thy" italicised.

The Great Divorce was first serialised in the Anglican newspaper The Guardian in 1944 and 1945 and published in book form in 1945; its title responds to Blake’s The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, and George MacDonald appears as the narrator’s guide, a role compared to Virgil’s for Dante.
The Internet Archive holds the 1946 New York: Macmillan edition of The Great Divorce as an access-restricted item whose text is not downloadable.

C. S. Lewis was born 29 November 1898 in Belfast and died 22 November 1963 in Oxford; he taught at Magdalen College, Oxford from 1925 and held the Cambridge chair of Medieval and Renaissance Literature from 1954.
